note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Severe "blinding" headache for 3 days; no clear trigger or exposure reported.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Sudden onset on waking 3 days ago; persistent continuous pain partially relieved by ibuprofen (from ~8/10 to ~5/10).
  - Pain generalized, stronger over the right eye; photophobia and intermittent "shooting lights" (visual phenomena).
  - Feels "a bit sick" but no vomiting; sleeps through night and not woken by headache.
  - Occasional stabbing pain when standing up quickly or moving head.
- ENT symptoms:
  - Throat swelling/closure sensation: denied.
  - Voice change/hoarseness: denied.
  - Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: denied.
  - Nasal symptoms/sinus pain: denied.
  - Ocular: photophobia and intermittent visual disturbances described as "shooting lights."
  - Stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea: denied.
  - Facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling: denied.
  - Ear pain/hearing changes, neck pain/swelling: denied.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - Occasional prior mild, short headaches historically; no prior prolonged headaches like this.
  - Family history: mother has severe migraines (with vomiting).
  - Pharmacy BP check ~1 year ago was reported as normal.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: none reported.
  - Current medications: combined oral contraceptive pill (started ~1 year ago; name not documented); occasional ibuprofen PRN for headache.
  - Rescue/other meds: paracetamol discussed as allowable concurrently (not yet started/prescribed).
- Social/context:
  - Lives alone; works from home; drinks alcohol approximately once weekly. No smoking or recreational drug use reported.
  - Patient was alone during the consultation.

Objective:
- Observable swelling/distribution: none reported.
- Airway/breathing descriptors: none reported.
- Mental status and associated features: alert, oriented; no syncope or loss of consciousness reported.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient: patient alone.

Assessment:
- Working clinical impression:
  - Probable migraine (possible migraine with visual aura) — most likely given photophobia, visual phenomena, family history, and partial analgesic response.
- Evidence summary from transcript:
  - Sudden-onset severe headache on waking, continuous for 3 days; photophobia and intermittent visual "shooting lights"; partial relief with ibuprofen; no fever, no focal neurologic deficits; family history of migraine.
- Differential diagnosis (top 2–3 from provided DDx, aligned with transcript):
  1. Migraine (probable migraine with visual aura) — High likelihood.
     - Justification: Photophobia and visual phenomena, severe headache interfering with function, partial response to analgesia, positive family history.
     - Opposing evidence: Continuous severe headache for 3 days without clear stereotyped transient aura and persistent pain warrants exclusion of secondary causes.
  2. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) — Medium likelihood.
     - Justification: Young woman on combined oral contraceptive pill (pro-thrombotic risk) with subacute progressive headache and visual symptoms; some positional/stabbing element reported.
     - Opposing evidence: No focal neurologic signs, no documented papilledema, and no other VTE features currently reported.
  3. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) — Medium likelihood.
     - Justification: Young woman with persistent headache and visual disturbances; fundoscopy/exam pending.
     - Opposing evidence: No documented papilledema, no pulsatile tinnitus reported, and onset was abrupt over days rather than weeks — exam and imaging needed.
- Conflict noted:
  - None significant between transcript and DDx; DDx appropriately includes secondary causes to be excluded given continuous severe headache.

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised:
  - Provider recommended booking an in-person appointment via support team for full neurological examination and fundoscopy (patient instructed to book; appointment planned).
  - Provider offered to prescribe a stronger NSAID (described as "similar to ibuprofen but stronger") to replace current ibuprofen and advised that paracetamol may be taken concurrently; take with food. (Prescription to be arranged when patient books appointment / per clinician process.)
  - Advised to go to Emergency Department (A&E) urgently if headache becomes unbearable, markedly worse, changes character, or new focal neurologic signs occur.
- Specific patient/caregiver instructions:
  - Book and attend the arranged in-person appointment for neurological exam and fundoscopy.
  - If symptoms worsen (see escalation criteria) present to A&E immediately.
  - Continue to avoid triggers as known; continue current medications as discussed until review.
  - If migraine with aura is confirmed, contraception may need reassessment — clinician will check blood pressure and consider suitability of current pill during follow-up.
- Escalation criteria / red flags (patient advised to seek urgent care if any occur):
  - New or worsening focal neurologic deficits (weakness, numbness, speech changes, visual loss).
  - Sudden severe worsening ("worst ever" or thunderclap), loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, neck stiffness, new confusion.
  - Headache becoming unbearable or not responding to advised measures.
- Follow-up and referrals:
  - In-person neurological and ophthalmologic (fundoscopy) examination planned at booked appointment.
  - Consider urgent neuroimaging (CT head ± CT venography or MRI/MR venography) if any red flags develop or if exam/fundoscopy suggests raised intracranial pressure or secondary cause (recommendation informed by DDx; consistent with need to exclude CVST/SAH/IIH).
  - Contraceptive review at follow-up if migraine with aura is determined.
  - No ENT/allergy referral indicated from transcript.
- Other:
  - Auto-injector discussion / allergy plans: not applicable / not discussed.
  - COVID-19 vaccine suitability: not discussed.

Quality checks / document_quality:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (blood pressure, pulse, temperature) not recorded.
  - Neurological examination findings and fundoscopy not yet performed.
  - Exact name/type of the combined oral contraceptive pill not documented.
  - Specific prescribed medication name, dose, and duration not documented (clinician offered to prescribe but prescription details not recorded).
  - Any baseline weight/BMI (relevant for IIH) not recorded.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None substantive; DDx appropriately broadens differential to include CVST/IIH/SAH as secondary causes to exclude given persistent severe headache.
- Transcript quality:
  - Initial audio volume issue noted but overall consultation content was intelligible; minor inaudible segments where specific pill name was not captured.
